Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe the diagnostic findings of acute compartment syndrome in adults.
Describe the diagnostic findings of acute compartment syndrome in children.
Identify the risk factors for compartment syndrome.
Describe the pathophysiology of compartment syndrome.
Define the natural history of compartment syndrome.
Develop treatment plans for the management of compartment syndrome.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview




NOTES

Muscular compartment volume is relatively fixed because of the low compliance of the
myofascial envelope.
The pathophysiology of acute compartment syndrome (ACS) represents a vicious cycle: injury
→ inflammation/edema, hemorrhage → increased compartment pressure → decreased
circulation (inflow, outflow, lymphatics) → ischemia/tissue damage → increased
edema/vascular permeability → additional increase in pressure → additional injury → and so
forth.
Time from injury is important.
4 hours: reversible ischemia
6 hours: ischemic necrosis with permanent damage (muscle fibrosis, dysesthesias, weakness)
Prolonged (>8 hours): extensive muscle death → adverse sequelae (including
rhabdomyolysis) → renal failure → amputation/death (rare), permanent nerve injury
1
Epidemiology
200,000 cases per year, usually related to trauma
1
Approximately 75% of cases are associated with fractures.2
Of these, 36% are tibial shaft fractures.2
Overall incidence in patients with a tibial shaft fracture ranges from 2% to 24%.2,3
Most common cause of malpractice suits against orthopaedic surgeons4
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Vasculature

Vasculature
Compartment syndrome is a pathophysiologic process that causes failure of the
microvasculature within myoneural tissue but does not affect blood flow through large
vasculature. Therefore, distal pulses typically are not affected. Venous congestion,
including acute proximal venous thrombosis, is a rare cause of ACS (phlegmasia cerulea
dolens).1
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000657
2/33

Nerves

Nerves
In general, neural tissue is considered particularly sensitive to ischemia, because sensory
nerves are more susceptible than motor nerves. Therefore, paresthesias are an early
sign of ACS.
Musculature

Musculature
Muscle is a very metabolically active tissue and is particularly sensitive to ischemia. The
onset of muscular hypoxia typically is heralded by intense pain, and pain out of
proportion to otherwise expected findings is the hallmark finding of ACS. As muscle
ischemia progresses to tissue injury, muscle enzymes, including creatine phosphokinase
and myoglobin, are released. This is known as rhabdomyolysis, which may result in
severe renal injury. Extensive muscle death may lead to rhabdomyolysis and, in turn,
renal failure, which may result in amputation and (rarely) death.
Etiology
Trauma

Trauma
Trauma is the most common cause of ACS, most often occurring in boys and men aged
14 to 39 years.1,2 Approximately two-thirds of patents with ACS have an associated
fracture, most commonly occurring in the leg and associated with fractures of the tibial
shaft.2 The next most common site is the forearm, which is associated with fractures of
the distal radius, again most common in young males.2 Although distal radial fractures
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000657
3/33

are the injury most commonly associated with forearm compartment syndrome, the
percentage of distal radius fractures associated with compartment syndromes is low.
Acute carpal tunnel syndrome also can occur with distal radius fracture, and it should be
distinguished from ACS of the forearm. Crush injury without fracture also may result in
ACS.2,5
Reperfusion

Reperfusion
Reperfusion injury after limb revascularization may lead to compartment syndrome.
Prophylactic fasciotomy of the leg often is performed at the time of vascular repair of
acute arterial occlusion. So-called well-leg compartment syndrome is a reported
complication of prolonged surgical management with the leg in the lithotomy or other
elevated position.
Found-Down Compartment Syndrome

Found-Down Compartment Syndrome
A third common scenario is found-down compartment syndrome, which occurs after
prolonged unconsciousness or immobility, such as after drug overdose, in which body
weight compresses the dependent muscle groups and causes prolonged ischemia.6,7
Exercise

Exercise
Exercise is associated with two forms of compartment syndrome: acute exercise-induced
compartment syndrome (also referred to as exertional or traumatic rhabdomyolysis)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000657
4/33

and chronic exertional compartment syndrome. Exercise-induced compartment
syndrome is a fulminant process that results in severe pain, swelling, and potential
neurologic compromise (as is typically associated with other forms of ACS); however, the
diagnosis may not be considered because of the absence of trauma and lack of
understanding that intense, repetitive muscle contraction can cause ACS. A classic
activity associated with acute exertional compartment syndrome is intense weightlifting.
Similar to other forms of ACS, the management of exercise-induced compartment
syndrome is immediate fasciotomy.8,9
So-called chronic exertional compartment syndrome is a self-limited condition causing
pain in the leg that occurs with exercise and resolves spontaneously with rest, often
occurring with repetitive activities, such as running. Therefore, the name is somewhat of
a misnomer because the symptoms are present intermittently rather than chronically.
Similar to ACS, evidence and consensus regarding diagnostic criteria and indications for
surgical management are lacking; however, emergent surgical management of this
condition is not necessary.
Natural History
The natural history of unmanaged compartment syndrome leads to well-recognized
dysfunction of the affected extremity, including variable paresthesia, paralysis, and fibrosis.10
Typical findings according to the affected region include the following:
Hand: claw hand/intrinsic-minus contracture, manifested by hyperextension of the
metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion of the interphalangeal joints of all lesser digits
(Figure 1)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000657
5/33

Figure 1 Illustrations of a finger show progressive intrinsic contracture (red). A, Normal range of
the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint with the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint extended and
the intrinsics stretched. Panels B and C show a mildly contracted intrinsic muscle. B, The MCP
joint is extended, the contracted intrinsic is stretched, and the PIP joint cannot flex. C, The MCP
joint is flexed, the contracted intrinsic is relaxed, and PIP joint flexion is possible. D, A severely
contracted intrinsic muscle. The MCP joint is driven into flexion, and the PIP joint is driven into
extension. (Reproduced from Tosti R, Thoder JJ, Ilyas AM: Intrinsic contracture of the hand:
diagnosis and management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2013;21[10]:581-591.)
Forearm: Volkmann ischemic contracture
The clinical manifestation varies depending on the affected muscle.
Usually includes flexion contractures of the fingers, flexion contracture of the wrist, limited
pronation and supination of the forearm, and often intrinsic-minus positioning of the hand.
Anterior leg—Injury to the peroneal nerve and loss of anterior compartment function may
result in footdrop caused by loss of active ankle dorsiflexion. 
Typically occurs after débridement of the anterior compartment
However, if anterior leg compartment syndrome is unmanaged, resultant ischemic
contracture of the leg also may result in ankle stiffness or dorsiflexion contracture of the
ankle.
Posterior leg
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000657
6/33

Unmanaged compartment syndrome of the deep posterior compartment affects the flexor
hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus, and tibialis posterior muscles about the ankle.
Contracture of these muscles will cause clawing of the toes and ankle stiffness.
Foot
Unmanaged compartment syndrome of the foot results in loss of function and possible
contracture of the intrinsic muscles of the foot. 
Common outcomes include fixed flexion deformity and numbness of the toes.
With timely diagnosis and management, the natural history of compartment syndrome often
can be altered, with damage and dysfunction minimized.
Risk Factors
Young age1,2,11
Male sex
Prolonged hypotension
Complex, butterfly, or segmental tibia shaft fractures
Bicondylar tibial plateau fractures
High-energy distal radius fracture
Ipsilateral distal radius and elbow injuries
Pediatric tibial tubercle fracture
Crush injuries
Prolonged ischemia or vascular injury
Prolonged prone or lithotomy positioning

Risk Factors
Compartment syndrome is a common musculoskeletal pathology. Excessive pressure in
extremity compartments may lead to tissue injury and death. If detected early in its
course, the natural history of compartment syndrome can be altered and sequalae can
be avoided. Compartment syndrome may be encountered by any physician, given the
breadth of etiologies that have been reported. These etiologies include trauma; fracture;
thermal injury; narcotic or drug use; infiltrations; lithotomy, intraoperative positioning, or
prolonged positioning of an immobile or unconscious patient; constricting dressings or
casts; nephrotic syndrome; rhabdomyolysis; bleeding disorders; infusions; andSEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000657
7/33

infections.1,10 Several specific fracture patterns have been associated with compartment
syndrome.
Regardless of the etiology, the common pathology leads to a predictable vicious cycle,
beginning with inflammation, swelling, pressure, and altered circulation. This causes
cellular damage and increased vascular permeability, leading to additional swelling,
pressure, and tissue damage. Tissue damage becomes irreversible over a short time,
and sequelae become unavoidable. The sequelae of skeletal muscle necrosis and
physiologic overload of tissue degradation products may result in damage to the kidneys
and other organ systems and may result in death.
Classification
ACS is classified according to etiology as follows:
Acute
Unknown duration (also referred to as found-down compartment syndrome)
Evolved
Acute exercise-induced (also referred to as acute or traumatic rhabdomyolysis)
Acutely elevated compartment pressures from intense muscular exertion without any
other traumatic event that, after present, behaves similar to any other ACS and results in
rhabdomyolysis and loss of compartment function
Should be diagnosed and managed as ACS

Classification
To determine the best treatment option, compartment syndrome is classified according
to the duration of elevated pressure and potential sequelae. The term ACS refers to a
developing compartment syndrome with increased pressures that lead to tissue
dysfunction and, ultimately, irreversible damage within as little as 6 hours. Compartment
syndrome of unknown duration describes a patient in whom it remains unknown
whether tissue damage is reversible or irreversible because the time of onset is
unknown. This may happen after prolonged loss of consciousness and/or prolonged
immobility, such as after a drug or alcohol overdose, a fall from which the patient cannot
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000657
8/33

get up (such as in Parkinson disease), or after being trapped in a building collapse. In
evolved compartment syndrome, tissue damage has entered the irreversible damage
phase, consistent with the natural history of ACS.
Although uncommon, an acute event of compartment syndrome can result of exercising
aggressively.9 This is an example of compartment syndrome without a traumatic event,
and it can be diagnosed and managed the same as ACS resulting from a traumatic event.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
General Considerations

General Considerations
Orthopaedic surgeons should maintain a high index of suspicion for ACS in evaluating
any patient with a fracture or crush injury to the limb or who complains of unexplained
extremity pain after activity, even if not associated with obvious injury.1 The examiner
should note any skin changes, such as blistering. Serial documented examinations by the
same examiners aid in monitoring for changes. Patients who report increasing pain or
loss of ability to move the extremity should be promptly reexamined. The diagnosis of
ACS is based on a constellation of physical examination findings and requires an alert
patient who can provide a reliable history and cooperate with repeated physical
examinations. Patients with altered mental status who cannot provide a reliable history
and cooperate with clinical examinations pose a particular change to diagnosis. If
concern exists that such a patient has compartment syndrome, compartment pressures
can be measured. Such measurements should not delay surgical management if the
clinical diagnosis is apparent (Resource 1).
The authors of this lesson err toward potential overdiagnosis of compartment syndrome
because ACS is one of the few limb- and life-threatening conditions in orthopaedic
surgery. Outcomes are best if early fasciotomy is performed. The disadvantages of over-
management are considered acceptable and include scarring, potential muscle
weakness, increased risk of infection, requirements for additional procedures or
management, and extended hospitalization with greater cost of care.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000657
9/33

The diagnosis of ACS generally is based on the presence of multiple clinical findings,
known as the six Ps. These clinical findings are nonspecific;12 therefore, repeat
examinations are critical to recognize subtle changes in a timely manner. The sensitivity
of the clinical findings improves if three or more findings are present.12
Pain out of proportion/pain with passive stretch
Most reliable clinical symptom
Generally, if findings other than pain are present, the diagnosis has been delayed.
Paresthesias
Often, neurologic deficits in the injured limb are noted on admission and may be
caused by the associated trauma. 
However, progressive sensory loss or the onset of paresthesias in a nerve that
traverses the involved compartment may be an early sign of ACS, occurring within 6
hours. 
Surgeon should refrain from ruling out ACS based on normal neurologic findings
because peripheral nerves vary in their anatomy and physiology.
Pallor: pale color of the extremity
Poikilothermia: coolness of the extremity
Pulselessness: more relevant for vascular injuries; not present in typical ACS.
Paralysis: late finding only
Pediatric ACS
Children have higher resting intramuscular pressure and lower blood pressure compared with
adults. ACS in children manifests in different clinical scenarios and may be associated with
different signs and symptoms than in adults. 
In the pediatric population, the three As are considered more predictive of acute limb
compartment syndrome and facilitate earlier diagnosis than the classic adult findings.11 These
clinical signs are as follows:
Anxiety
Analgesic needs increasing
Agitation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000657
10/33

Patient History

Patient History
Because ACS typically is associated with trauma, the clinician should understand the
mechanism and timing of associated injuries and the relevant medical history (use of
anticoagulants, diabetes mellitus or other illness associated with peripheral neuropathy
or vascular disease).
The clinician also should obtain the patient’s history of pain since injury and note
increasing pain or requests for analgesia.
Physical Examination
Most important diagnostic tool
Serial examinations recommended for high-risk individuals (recommended every 2 to 4 hours,
depending on index of suspicion)
Compressibility
The involved compartment often is described as soft or tense/firm.
This should be discouraged because evidence shows that palpation is unreliable.13
Pain with passive stretch: may be affected by adjacent fractures or impossible to perform in a
limb that is splinted or immobilized with an external fixator
Compartment Pressure Measurement
Involves inserting a needle into the involved compartment to attain direct pressure
measurement (Resource 1)
Typically performed for equivocal physical examination findings and/or in obtunded patients
but should not delay surgical management if the diagnosis is apparent based on clinical
findings alone
Intracompartmental pressure varies within the compartment.
Should be evaluated within 5 cm of fracture, the location at which pressures have been
shown to be highest14
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000657
11/33

Thresholds for fasciotomy can be based on absolute pressures (usually >30 to 40 mm Hg) or
more typically perfusion pressure.10
Perfusion pressure is the difference between diastolic blood pressure and
intracompartmental pressure.
Considered more accurate than use of absolute pressure but is nonspecific for the
diagnosis of ACS, regardless of the specific threshold used15
Consistent perfusion pressure values lower than 30 mm Hg increase concern for
compartment syndrome.10
Absolute, one-time pressure measurements overestimate diagnosis.
For an anesthetized patient, pre-sedation diastolic blood pressure should be used, unless the
procedure is expected to continue for a prolonged period (eg, >4 hours).
Continuous compartment pressure monitoring with an indwelling catheter may further
improve accuracy.
Neurovascular Examination
Nerves

Nerves
The clinician should assess sensation and motor function of the nerves that traverse
each compartment. Knowledge of the anatomic course of extremity nerves is necessary
to relate findings in a given peripheral nerve to a specific muscle compartment. For
example, paresthesias or sensory loss in the following lower leg nerves are indicative of
possible ACS in the associated leg compartment (Table 1).

Superficial posterior

Posterior tibial
Plantar surface of foot
Deep posterior

Musculature

Musculature
Manual motor testing should be performed and compared with that of the contralateral
leg if possible. The examiner should be cognizant that apparent muscle weakness may
be related to the associated injury, pain, sedation, nerve dysfunction, or primary muscle
injury.
Vasculature

Vasculature
Limb warmth is assessed, and distal pulses are evaluated. The absence of pulses is a late
finding or may be because baseline vascular disease, hypotension, or another associated
(and possibly unknown) injury.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiography is indicated in a limb in which compartment syndrome is suspected, primarily to
rule out an associated fracture or joint dislocation.
Computed Tomography
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000657
13/33


Computed Tomography
CT may be useful in identifying a vascular injury. Other options include angiography in
interventional radiology or visual identification in the operating room. Advanced imaging
modalities, such as MRI and CT, do not play a current role in the diagnosis of ACS;
however, they may be indicated for the management of other pathology. Regardless,
delayed surgical release of compartments should be avoided.
Differential Diagnosis
The following conditions should be considered and ruled out in a patient with acute extremity
pain and swelling:
Acute deep vein thrombosis
Cellulitis
Necrotizing soft-tissue infections
Gas gangrene
Peripheral vascular injury
Rhabdomyolysis
These conditions also are limb- and life-threatening problems that require management
different from that for ACS.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Limbs at risk for ACS should not be elevated or kept in a dependent position.
No role exists for nonsurgical management of ACS. Hyperbaric oxygen and osmotic diuresis
(eg, use of mannitol) have been studied as adjuncts to therapy; however, no current evidence
supports their routine use.
Missed/late compartment syndrome: more than 48 hours since presumed onset, with
evidence of neuromuscular deficit
Controversial16,17
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000657
14/33

Generally nonsurgical; fasciotomy for late evolved compartment syndrome is associated with
increased rate of infection, wound-healing problems, and high risk for amputation.16
Exception: pediatric patients11,12
Rarely, ACS may be managed nonsurgically in a limb without function (eg, the leg in a patient
with complete paraplegia)
Surgical Management
The surgical management of ACS involves fasciotomy of all involved compartments.
Indications
Diagnosis of ACS in a pediatric or adult patient less than 6 to 8 hours since the onset of critical
elevated pressure
Delayed diagnosis of compartment syndrome in a pediatric patient11
Relative indication for patients with indeterminate timing, especially if minimal evidence of
permanent tissue injury is observed11 (Videos 1 through 4)

Contraindications
Missed or evolved compartment syndrome: controversial (more than 48 hours without
function)7,16,17

Contraindications
The goal is to diagnose compartment syndrome early while the patient is in the acute
phase and to intervene while damage is reversible, therefore altering the natural history.
Evidence of irreversible myoneural injury is observed in some patients at the time of
diagnosis because of late presentation or failure to recognize the early symptoms.
Fasciotomy does not revive necrotic muscle and may cause more harm than benefit by
exposing devitalized tissue.7Complications of fasciotomy are high if necrotic muscle is
encountered. Although this is controversial, expert consensus recommends supportive
management, with a focus on minimizing systemic complications and preventing
contracture7 (Resource 1). Releasing compartments in patients with evolved
compartment syndrome may lead to physiologic shock caused by systemic release of
inflammatory mediators and is associated with sepsis and high late amputation rates.7,7
Some studies advocate for consideration of release, aggressive débridement, and
reconstruction in the pediatric forearm.17 Importantly, children with compartment
syndrome have an increased capacity for tissue preservation. In contrast to adult
patients, delayed release of compartments (more than 12 hours after injury) has not
been demonstrated to result in poorer outcomes in pediatric patients.11
Fasciotomy
The goal is to normalize compartment pressure before irreversible myoneural tissue damage
occurs.
If fracture fixation will be performed at a later date, the clinician should consider the location
of incisions for the next surgical procedure without compromising the goal of compartment
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:42 AM
AAOS | Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000657
18/33

release.
After fasciotomy, the skin and fascia must be left open with a sterile dressing.
The patient should return to the operating room after 48 to 72 hours for débridement of
nonviable tissue, if encountered.
Primary closure typically is performed 4 to 5 days later; a split-thickness skin graft can be
performed after 7 days if closure is not possible.
Early closure is associated with recurrent compartment syndrome.
The clinician should prioritize closure of incisions to cover exposed bone (eg, medial leg
wound).
Leg
Four compartments: anterior, lateral, superficial posterior, deep posterior (Figure 2 )
The anterior compartment is almost always involved; the lateral compartment is the second
compartment commonly involved.
Deep posterior compartment syndrome is the most difficult to diagnose on physical
examination; it results in clawfoot if unmanaged.
Single- and dual-incision fasciotomies are associated with equivalent outcomes.
Dual-incision fasciotomy (Figure 3)
Medial incision: superficial and deep posterior
Lateral incision: anterior and lateral
Single-incision fasciotomy (Figure 4)—After making a lateral incision, the surgeon accesses
all compartments laterally by raising a flap and then releases the deep posterior
compartment from the fibular attachment (Video 5).

Forearm
The forearm consists of three anatomic muscle compartments: volar, dorsal, and
lateral/mobile wad (Figure 5).
The volar compartment is most common the compartment involved; isolated dorsal
compartment syndrome is rare.
A volar incision usually is adequate to decompress the entire forearm, unless a crushing
component is present; the carpal tunnel typically also is released.
Compression of the median nerve is possible at four sites. In addition to releasing the
median nerve at the carpal tunnel, the clinician must assess these other sites to determine
the need for possible release.18
Lacertus fibrosis
Pronator teres
Proximal deep surface of the flexor digitorum superficialis
Carpal tunnel

A dorsal incision is used to release the dorsal compartment if a crush injury is present and
pressures remain elevated after release of the volar compartment.
The carpal tunnel typically is released as a part of a forearm compartment release.

Arm
Anterior and posterior compartments can be released via a lateral or medial incision. Direct
incisions over the compartments also may be used.19
The surgeon can release the deltoid laterally, if necessary (Video 6).

Thigh
Three compartments: anterior, medial, posterior
Single lateral incision (anterior and posterior compartments); additional medial incision (may
be required for the medial compartment).
Foot
Nine compartments
Surgical release is controversial because of the morbidity associated with release.
Release changes foot morphology, infection risk, wound-healing issues
Nonsurgical management may result in neuropathy and claw toes.
Alternatively, pie crust multiple stab incisions in strategic locations may effectively
decompress all involved compartments; nonadherent bolster dressings or a vacuum-assisted
closure device may be placed. Subsequent suture closure is not required.
Gluteal

Tense gluteal compartment
Fasciotomy may result in great morbid if necrotic abductors are encountered.
Progressive sciatic nerve dysfunction is an indication for release.
Hand
Difficult to diagnose because of complex anatomy and because no nerves are associated with
intrinsic muscle compartments that can be tested for early neural dysfunction19,20
Anatomically, the hand has 10 compartments.
Considerable hand swelling is common after injury, whereas compartment syndrome of the
hand is not; whether compartment release is beneficial remains unclear.
The classic hand fasciotomy consists of four incisions and an associated carpal tunnel release.
Four dorsal/three volar interossei released via incisions over the dorsal second and fourth
metacarpals
Adductor pollicis released via second metacarpal incision radially and deep
Thenar muscles released via direct incision
Hypothenar muscles released via direct incision
Carpal tunnel release may be considered; however, acute carpal tunnel syndrome is more
commonly associated with wrist and forearm injury than hand trauma.
Controversies in hand management
Whether fasciotomies in the hand are beneficial remains unclear; indications for release,
other than the median nerve, are unclear.
For the digits, some surgeons advocate release over the noncontact side of finger to avoid
nerve/vessel dysfunction.11,19,20
Release procedures
Thumb: radial incision
Index and long fingers: ulnar incision
Ring and little fingers: radial incision
Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Incomplete fascial release will not decrease intracompartmental pressure and is ineffective in
mitigating ACS.
Fasciotomy incisions may limit the placement of later incisions necessary for fracture fixation;
this can be minimized via careful planning of fasciotomy incisions.

Tensioner: refers to numerous techniques and devices that engage and are used to apply

Postoperative Management
The patient should return to the operating room approximately every 48 hours for
assessment of the affected compartment for additional nonviable tissue. Several
methods can be used to attain eventual closure or coverage of the wound. The wound
can be sequentially closed on return trips to the operating room, with eventual primary
closure as swelling subsides. Another option involves the use a tensioner device that is
sequentially tightened until the fasciotomy edges are approximated. The pie-crust
method involves making several relaxing incisions over another compartment so the
fasciotomy incision can be primarily closed and the pie-crust incisions can heal via
secondary intention. After the wound bed requires no additional débridement for
nonviable tissue, a split-thickness skin graft can be used to attain final coverage.
Range of motion and suppleness of the affected extremity and joints should be
maintained. This can be achieved via physical and occupational therapy and home
exercise programs. Casts, splints, and braces also are used to hold the affected
extremity in a functional position. Care should be taken to avoid skin irritation or

Social Complications
Compartment syndrome is one of the most common reasons for litigation against orthopaedic
surgeons. Plaintiff awards often are associated with inadequate or incomplete documentation
of clinical findings and decision making.
Nonunion
Four-compartment fasciotomy in patients with a tibial shaft or plateau fracture is associated
with a considerable increase in nonunion (20% versus 5%).21/li>
Pain as an Illness
Many years after release of compartment syndrome, approximately 10% of patients report
troublesome pain in the affected extremity, many of whom seek treatment specifically for the
pain.
Infection
Four-compartment fasciotomy in patients with a tibial shaft or plateau fracture is associated
with infection (20% versus 4%).21 The risk for infection is increased further in patients with
delayed diagnosis or delayed fasciotomy if necrotic tissue is encountered.
Stiffness
Limbs managed via fasciotomy often are splinted to stabilize the limb, including any associated
fractures. Depending on associated injuries, patients may not be allowed to bear weight early.

Splinting can prevent contractures, such as equinus of the ankle.
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Nerve palsy is common because of the natural history of evolved compartment syndrome.
According to a clinical series , as many as 18% of patients have a footdrop.22
The Tsuge classification system for Volkmann ischemic contracture in the forearm describes
complications. The Tsuge classification describes residual function as mild (fingers only),
moderate (fingers and wrist), and severe (contracture and neurologic compromise of dorsal
and volar compartments).23
Outcomes
Overall poorer health outcomes, with long-term effects on quality of life, are noted in patients
with inadequately managed compartment syndrome.
Outcomes are better in patients who are satisfied with the cosmetic appearance of the limb,
patients with a fasciotomy that did not require a skin graft, and patients with a wound that was
closed more quickly.22
Compared with patients who have injuries similar to compartment syndrome, patients with
compartment syndrome who undergo fasciotomy have an increased hospital length of stay,
infection rate, time to healing (skin and bone), and cost of care.22
